assertions.description: The central contract of this feature, stated as an assertion so it stays true: no plausible surface exposes a safety verdict to a page. A detectable warning would be a defeatable one — a page could behave differently when it knew it was being judged.
assertions.test: (()=>{try{const absent=(path)=>{const parts=path.split('.');let current=globalThis;for(const part of parts){if(current==null)return true;current=current[part];}return current===undefined;};return ['navigator.safeBrowsing','navigator.securityState','document.suspiciousSiteWarning','window.chrome.safeBrowsing'].every(absent);}catch(e){return false;}})()

assertions.description: The control that makes the assertion above worth anything: the same technique must find something that exists and miss something that does not. Without it, a broken probe and a genuine absence are the same result.

ReportingObserver and CSP violation events are real, and are regularly mistaken for a safety channel. They carry information outward from your page to you, which is the opposite direction — asserted so the distinction the demo draws rests on something checkable.

The audit tool parses pasted markup with DOMParser, which builds a document without running scripts or loading subresources. Anything else would make a tool for auditing suspicious markup dangerous to use.

The trap the links page fell into: new URL() accepts nonsense and percent-encodes it into a hostname rather than throwing. A tool that builds links from user input has to check the hostname shape separately.

Why the insecure-subresource check looks only at absolute http:// URLs. On a plain-http development server every relative path resolves to http, which made this page report three findings against itself until the check was narrowed.
